references.text: The Lord saw that Leah was unloved and opened her womb. This is the direct occasion for Reuben's birth.
The angel tells Hagar that the Lord has heard her misery, and she shall name her son Ishmael. The same pattern of naming based on God's intervention in suffering.
God remembered Rachel and opened her womb, paralleling how the Lord intervened for Leah in her unloved state.
Reuben is mentioned as Jacob's firstborn, Leah's son, in the complete genealogy of Jacob's twelve sons.
The Lord says, 'I have seen my people's misery' (rā'āh ʿŏnî) - the same expression Leah uses: 'The Lord has seen my misery.'
God saw the Israelites and knew their suffering. A thematic parallel to how the Lord saw Leah's affliction.
'See my misery and my pain' - a prayer that mirrors Leah's experience of the Lord seeing her suffering.
Shows the development from Leah's hope to be loved (Reuben) to her feeling honored (Zebulun).
Rachel's expression 'God has heard my voice' mirrors Leah's 'The Lord has seen my misery,' highlighting God's response to both women's suffering.
Highlights the parallel between Leah and Hannah as women who were 'seen' by God in their barrenness and named sons in gratitude for answered prayer.
Highlights the parallel between Eve and Leah as mothers who receive new sons as God's answer to earlier loss and suffering.
Immanuel ('God with us') is the ultimate fulfillment of Leah's prayer that the Lord would see her and be present.
